names.name: Śiva (Pinākin) in the invocations of early Naiyāyikas

descriptions: A distinct self (ātmāntara) qualified by virtues: free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness; endowed with merit, knowledge and concentration; possessing eightfold lordship (NBh 4.1.21).
He assists human effort and brings about the fruits of action; as a father to his children, so is He to beings (NBh 4.1.21).

The all-knowing, imperishable maker proved from the world's effecthood, the combining of atoms, support and destruction, traditional skills, the validity of the Veda, scripture, the Veda's sentences and special number (NK 5.1).
Reasoning about Him is itself worship; worship of Him is the path to heaven and liberation (NK 1.2–1.3).
The one whom all schools worship under different names — Śiva, Puruṣottama, the Grandfather, the omniscient, the unobstructed … (NK stabaka 1, opening prose).
Author of the Veda, whose validity rests on its being rooted in His perception (Gaṅgeśa).
negations: free of demerit (adharma), false knowledge (mithyājñāna) and heedlessness (pramāda) (NBh 4.1.21)
not the material cause of atoms, selves, ākāśa, time, space or minds, which are eternal
relation_to_self: Īśvara is one self among many eternal, all-pervading selves — a special self. Individual selves are eternally distinct from Him and from each other; He makes their karma fruitful. Liberation is not union with Him but the self's absolute release from pain.
relation_to_world: Efficient cause of the world: He sets eternal atoms in motion according to the selves' merit and demerit and brings about dissolution; the world of substances, qualities, motions, universals and relations is real, not an appearance.
caveat: Nyāya would reject reading 'one truth' as ontological monism: selves are eternally many and distinct from the Lord; atoms, ākāśa, time, space and minds are eternal reals not produced by Him; liberation is not merger. Udayana's statement that all schools worship one Lord under different names is made from within Nyāya theism and does not concede the other schools' doctrines; Buddhists and Mīmāṃsakas named there reject being so included. Nyāya also rejects any levels-of-truth reading of its own realism.

descriptions: Saluted as 'Īśvara, the cause' at the opening of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha; the knowledge that leads to the highest good arises from dharma manifested by His command.
By His will the world is dissolved at the end of a Brahmā's lifespan and created again for the selves' experience, through their adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The highest good (niḥśreyasa) is the fruit of dharma (VS 1.1.2): liberation, in which the self has no contact with a body (VS 5.2.20).
negations: the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra itself does not name Īśvara
relation_to_self: The Lord is a self distinct from the innumerable individual selves, each made distinct by its own ultimate particularity (viśeṣa).
relation_to_world: Efficient cause who initiates the motion of eternal atoms at creation and their separation at dissolution; the nine substances and the other categories are real.
caveat: Early Vaiśeṣika (the sūtras) does not explicitly name a Lord (scholarly account); theism appears from Praśastapāda on. The school would reject monism: innumerable eternal atoms, selves and minds, each individuated by ultimate particularity, are irreducibly many — the school's very name is traditionally linked with 'particularity'.

descriptions: The one omniscient supreme self; His cognition, desire and effort are eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
His convention 'from this word this meaning is to be understood' is the denotative power of words; all Vedic statements are valid because He spoke them (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Proved as the maker of earth, sprouts and the like because they are effects (Gaṅgeśa; Viśvanātha).
Viśvanātha salutes Kṛṣṇa as the seed of the tree of saṃsāra (Bhāṣāpariccheda 1).
negations: not the material cause of the world
no non-eternal cognition (His cognition is eternal)
relation_to_self: The supreme self is one of the two kinds of self; individual selves are distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
relation_to_world: Maker (efficient cause) of all effects; the categories are real and exactly definable.
caveat: As for Nyāya; in addition, Navya-Nyāya's analysis never admits a featureless or indeterminable ultimate, and it defends the exact definability of categories against Advaita's claim that they are indeterminable.
